items.title: Attachment classifications
items.claim: Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation (1970s) identified attachment styles in infants. In the original US sample, what proportion were classified as securely attached?
items.reveal_title: Roughly two thirds were classified secure
items.reveal:
Ainsworth (1978) reported about 66% secure, 22% insecure-avoidant, 12% insecure-resistant.

Main and Solomon (1990) later added a fourth category, disorganised attachment.
items.why: Distributions vary by culture. Van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg's 1988 meta-analysis showed cross-cultural variation in the proportions.

items.title: Bowlby's 44 thieves
items.claim: John Bowlby's 1944 '44 Juvenile Thieves' study linked maternal separation to later antisocial behaviour. What is a key methodological criticism made of it today?

options.text: The sample was very large and well controlled
Bowlby personally interviewed the children, risking confirmation bias, and the sample was small
It was a randomised controlled trial

items.reveal:
Bowlby studied 44 juvenile thieves and 44 controls at his clinic, conducting assessments himself. Critics note the risk of bias and the difficulty of separating maternal deprivation from broader disadvantage.

Rutter (1981) drew the influential distinction between privation and deprivation.
items.why: Foundational studies often used methods we would now strengthen, but they framed questions that still drive research.

items.title: Bowlby's monotropy claim has been substantially revised
items.claim: John Bowlby's original theory emphasised a single primary attachment figure (typically the mother). What does subsequent evidence suggest?

options.text: Monotropy is fully supported by all evidence

Infants form attachment hierarchies with multiple caregivers (Schaffer & Emerson 1964); fathers, grandparents and consistent non-parental carers can serve as attachment figures; quality matters more than exclusivity
Only mothers can be attachment figures

items.reveal:
Schaffer and Emerson's 1964 Glasgow study followed 60 babies and found by 18 months most had multiple attachments; nearly a third had primary attachment to someone other than the mother. Lamb's (2010) reviews of father involvement showed independent contributions to child outcomes.

The monotropy claim, alongside Bowlby's earlier ideas about 'maternal deprivation', shaped 1950s-60s policy (working mothers, daycare, hospital visiting). Rutter's 'Maternal Deprivation Reassessed' (1972) sharpened the distinction between privation (no attachment formed) and deprivation (loss of formed attachment).
items.why: Theories with policy implications need re-examination as evidence accumulates. Bowlby's core insight (attachment relationships matter) survives; the specific claim of monotropy has been substantially revised.
